book: A Philosophy of Software Design by John Ousterhout

chapters.title: 2 The Nature of Complexity
items: Complexity defined: anything related to the structure of a system that makes it hard to understand and modify
Complexity is weighted by where developers spend time (C = sum of c_p * t_p): isolating complexity where it's never seen is almost as good as eliminating it
Symptom: change amplification — a simple change requires modifications in many places
Symptom: cognitive load — how much a developer needs to know to complete a task
Symptom: unknown unknowns — not obvious what must change or what information is needed; the worst symptom
Cause: dependencies — code can't be understood or modified in isolation
Cause: obscurity — important information is not obvious
Complexity is incremental: it accumulates from many small dependencies and obscurities, so sweat the small stuff

chapters.title: 5 Information Hiding (and Leakage)
items: Information hiding: each module encapsulates design decisions/knowledge that don't appear in its interface
Red flag: Information Leakage — the same design decision/knowledge is reflected in multiple modules
Red flag: Temporal Decomposition — code structure follows execution order instead of information hiding
HTTP server example: reading and parsing a request split into separate classes leaks the request format; merge them
Classes can be made somewhat larger to hide information (too many small classes leak knowledge)
Red flag: Overexposure — an API forces users to learn rarely used features to use common ones
Defaults: interfaces should make the common case simple (e.g. HTTP response defaults)
Information hiding within a class: minimize the places each variable/detail is used
Taking it too far: don't hide information that is needed outside the module

chapters.title: 10 Define Errors Out Of Existence
items: Exception handling is a major source of complexity; handling code is hard to write and test
Too many exceptions: throwing is easy but pushes complexity onto callers
Define errors out of existence: design APIs so the error condition can't arise
Example: file deletion — Unix lets a deleted-while-open file keep working vs Windows refusing deletion
Example: Java substring throwing on out-of-range indexes instead of clamping
Mask exceptions: handle the exceptional condition at a low level so higher levels never see it (e.g. TCP retransmission, NFS retry)
Exception aggregation: handle many exceptions with a single handler in one place (web server dispatch example)
Just crash: for errors that are rare and not worth handling (e.g. out of memory), crash with diagnostics
Design special cases out of existence (e.g. text editor selection that always exists, represented as empty when nothing is selected)
Taking it too far: don't mask or define away errors whose information callers need
